title.narrative: Basic Education Quality and Access in Lao PDR program Phase 2 (BEQUAL Phase 2)

description.narrative: The Basic Education Quality and Access in Laos (BEQUAL) Program Phase 2 aims to improve primary student learning outcomes by focusing on teaching quality. BEQUAL Phase 2 strengthens the education system by advancing key national policy reforms in teaching practices, content and continuing professional development. It promotes inclusive education to address issues of inequality and inequity throughout its activities.

Basic Education Quality and Access in Lao PDR

description.narrative: A regional learning assessment, the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM) from 2019, provides the learning outcome baseline for all Grade 5 students in Laos who learned under the previous curriculum. Results showed that 2.5 per cent of Grade 5 students met the expected proficiency level in reading and 7.9 per cent in maths. Girls performed slightly better in reading and writing. Students who speak the language of instruction at home outperformed students who do not. Australia supports the Lao Government improve teaching quality and student learning outcomes through the Basic Education Quality and Access Program (BEQUAL). BEQUAL Phase 2 focuses on building the capacity of Lao primary teachers, enabling education inclusion and better learning in target districts. The 2024 SEA-PLM will provide insights on how Australian support through BEQUAL contributes to improve learning outcomes.

In April 2024, a baseline assessment of Grade 1 students’ Lao language skills was conducted as part of the Inclusive Teaching and Learning Study - a three-year longitudinal initiative. The study used the Early Grade Learning Assessment to evaluate listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills. A total of 883 students (52% girls) from 120 schools in 30 target districts across seven provinces supported by the Basic Education Quality and Access in Laos (BEQUAL) program participated. ‍ Findings show that 23% of students demonstrated high Lao literacy, including 25% of girls and 20% of boys. While results are comparable to earlier assessments, students from remote or non-Lao-speaking households continue to face significant learning challenges. ‍ BEQUAL is Australia’s flagship education initiative, supporting improved student learning outcomes by strengthening teaching quality, reforming the national primary curriculum, and promoting inclusive learning - particularly for disadvantaged students.

In May 2023, Lao PDR’s Ministry of Education and Sports conducted the national Grade 5 Assessment of Student Learning Outcomes (ASLO), providing a critical baseline of student achievement before the implementation of the new Grade 5 curriculum (September 2023). The assessment revealed serious learning gaps, particularly in mathematics, where only 1.1% of students reached minimum proficiency. Girls slightly underperformed boys (0.82% vs. 1.11%), and no disability-disaggregated data was reported. In reading, 23.4% of students achieved minimum proficiency, including 27.86% of girls and 19.27% of boys. ‍ The results highlight the urgent need for improvements, especially in numeracy. Notably, the mathematics test instrument was significantly more difficult than the reading assessment, which may have contributed to the very low scores. ‍ Australia supported the Ministry of Education and Sports to revise the national primary curriculum, including the Lao Language subject. Australia did not contribute to the development of the new mathematics curriculum. The ASLO results now serve as a baseline for measuring the impact of these reforms. Australia’s investment in curriculum reform and teacher professional development system strengthening have contributed to building the foundation for evidence-informed improvements in teaching and learning across the basic education sub-sector.

In September 2024, the Ministry of Education and Sports (MoES) adopted the Spoken Lao Program (SLP) as national policy to support Grade 1 students whose home language is not Lao. The program provides targeted oral language development to promote inclusive education from school entry, with support from Australia. ‍ Since Phase 1, BEQUAL co-designed, piloted, and evaluated SLP materials and training. Two pilot phases at increasing geographic scale, along with a rigorous study and endline evaluation, confirmed statistically significant learning gains in 2024—including for students with disabilities and learning difficulties. ‍ Based on this evidence, BEQUAL facilitated a national policy dialogue in July, leading to official approval of the Spoken Lao (SL) approach and materials for nationwide use. Australia funded the training of 15,613 educators (48% women) and the distribution of 184,680 student books and over 80,000 teaching aids. ‍ BEQUAL’s support in teacher orientation, Continuing Professional Development, and inclusive materials was key. Strategic communication highlighted the importance of mother tongue in acquiring Lao, leading to national recognition that SL must extend beyond Grade 1. ‍ The 2026-2030 Education and Sports Sector Development Plan prioritises support for non-Lao speaking learners. MoES now plans to expand SL to Grade 2 with continued BEQUAL support.

The BEQUAL program in Lao PDR is advancing inclusive education by ensuring all students, including those with disabilities, can access quality learning. A core strategy is collaborating with Organisations of Persons with Disabilities (OPDs), government bodies, and civil society to co-develop practical resources for teachers to use in the classroom. ‍ Teacher surveys (through BEQUAL monitoring) revealed a strong demand for hands-on professional development to support students with diverse disabilities. In response, BEQUAL is developing a Teacher Support Pack with OPDs’ guidance and Ministry of Education’s technical expertise. ‍ Modules on visual, hearing, and mobility impairments are complete, with one on intellectual disabilities underway. These modules, shaped by OPDs’ lived experiences, provide practical strategies for inclusive teaching. Teachers benefit from OPD-led sessions covering assistive devices, classroom adaptations, inclusive practices, and community engagement. Guidance on using local materials is also included. ‍ Key partners include the Inclusive Education Promotion Centre, Disability Services Center, National University of Laos, local schools, and technical experts like COPE and ADDP. This collaboration fosters mutual learning and systemic change, equipping teachers to better support all learners.

The Lao Government requested Australian support to establish a teacher professional development system in target areas. This built on Australia’s earlier support revising the national primary curriculum through the Basic Education Quality and Access in Laos (BEQUAL) program. Australia supports Lao teaching and learning at several levels, including focused capacity building at teacher training colleges, enabling school principals as learning leaders, and empowering teachers who bring the new curriculum alive. With Australia’s support and a contribution from the US Government, more teachers are accessing professional development in a cost-effective, context-relevant way. Over 90 per cent of teachers across 30 target districts received monthly professional development support this school year, with 61 per cent of these teachers showing improved teaching practices. Teachers with non-Lao speaking students reported almost 20 per cent more students managing Lao language work at grade level.
